title: Leader Joe Lichter, learning to read and helping each other
summary: Singing came from vaudeville. Joe Lichter led the band; older saxophonists helped Herman, a poor reader, and he comments on camaraderie among players.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: I see. Did you do any singing that early?
Oh, yeah, yeah. Because I sang -- that
Vaudeville, I see. Was there a leader that you recall, of this band?

Oh, yeah, his name was Joe Lichter. He was a man originally from Milwaukee, who had been a theatre conductor and a theatre musician most of his life. He'd done a lot of work in Chicago and he came back to Milwaukee. And he had the orchestra conductor at the Strand Theatre there for several years, and then when the theatres were getting a bit shaky, he switched to going to a ballroom, because he was basically a kind of a jazz player himself.
So it made it very much better for young people like myself to find a niche.
Did you learn anything about the kind of leadership functions from this man?

Oh, maybe, but -- and I was very -- I was so very much interested, as were most young musicians in being aware of everything that was happening around me and everything that was going down. And consequently, I think every one I ever worked for was some kind of influence on me. Maybe some influenced me to the point where I never wanted to be like they were, but that's the chance you take.
How did you get on this house band? Did they hear about you playing at school, or --

No, I think it was through some of the musicians in the band who were aware of me and knew I could do several things, and when the leader was looking for someone, they suggested (unintelligible) to him. Because I had some major weaknesses, like, my reading was very poor. Because I was never really in a position to read. I would practice and play the exercises and the chords and scales, and I would play and I would perform them.

So I had never really gotten around to a thing of having to read. And it was kind of a challenge the first few months, but the older people in the band, particularly the saxophone players, were kind enough to work with me and help me, right.
This kind of rubbed off through your career, a lot. Them helping you and you helping --

Well, I think that's prevalent in all of jazz music, particularly any music where you're supposedly creating something. One player will certainly help another, in 99 percent of the cases. And I think that feeling of camaraderie is a great thing.
How long were you on this house band?
Until the time I left Milwaukee, which would be my senior year in high school.
